title: Nor'easter Turns Streets into Rivers, Cancels Concerts Across the Northeast
summary:
A nor'easter — a powerful storm that sweeps in from the northeast — turned coastal streets into rivers across New York and New Jersey on Saturday, forcing states of emergency and cancelling everything from flights to concerts.

Tens of millions of people from Virginia to Maine were in the storm's path. The National Weather Service warned of "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall." In the New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan, floodwater inundated streets and homes. More than 100,000 households lost electricity, nearly all in the northeast.

Travel was chaotic. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 were grounded, according to FlightAware. The Federal Aviation Administration told passengers to check with airlines before heading to airports.

Saturday's full moon made things worse. The moon's gravitational pull raises ocean tides, and when a storm surge coincides with a full moon, coastal flooding can be significantly more severe. The National Weather Service urged people to "prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."

Officials sent urgent messages. "I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video, "Don't travel if you don't have to. Do not drive or walk through floodwater."

Major events were cancelled or moved. The Boston Red Sox shifted their final game against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. A professional soccer match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was called off. The Global Citizen Festival in Central Park — headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend — was cancelled. And Ed Sheeran's concert at Gillette Stadium near Boston was also scrapped for safety reasons.

The storm is part of a pattern of extreme weather affecting the region, though scientists continue to study how climate change influences individual storms. For now, residents are being told to stay off the roads and wait for the water to recede.
why_it_matters: Storms like this test the infrastructure millions of teenagers depend on — subways, power grids, schools and airports — and show how one weather system can cancel a concert, a ballgame and thousands of flights at once, raising hard questions about how coastal cities should adapt to a wetter, stormier future.

background_read: Nor'easters are a classic East Coast weather system: cold air from Canada collides with warm, moist air over the Atlantic, and the storm then tracks northeast along the coast — which is where the name comes from. The same setup produced the 1993 'Storm of the Century,' which dumped snow from the Gulf Coast to New England, and Hurricane Sandy in 2012, whose surge flooded parts of New York and New Jersey and led to years of rebuilding.

The National Weather Service (the US agency that issues forecasts and storm warnings) notes that coastal flooding is far worse when a surge arrives at high tide. The moon's gravity pulls the ocean higher during a full moon or new moon, a cycle some coastal planners call 'king tides.'

Many coastal cities have responded with sea walls, raised subway entrances, restored wetlands that absorb water and new flood maps. New York's subway, much of it underground and close to the harbour, remains one of the most flood-prone transit systems in the country.

perspectives.description: Emergency managers argue the warnings did their job: tens of millions of people were told in advance what was coming, states of emergency freed up money and crews, and schools, concerts and games were cancelled rather than putting crowds at risk. From this angle, the disruption is evidence that the system responded rather than failed.

Critics point out that flooded homes, lost power and paralysed airports hurt people who can least afford it: renters in basement apartments, hourly workers who lose pay, and small businesses that flood repeatedly. They also warn that each storm leaves behind damaged infrastructure that the next storm makes worse.

Analysts note that nor'easters are nothing new; what has changed is how much expensive development sits in low-lying coastal areas and how often these events now arrive. The full moon and storm surge combination is basic physics, and researchers caution that linking any single storm to climate change requires careful study rather than a quick answer.

Planners are asking whether sea walls, raised entrances, restored wetlands and better flood maps can keep pace, and whether transit systems should shut down sooner. The storm also raises a scheduling question: how many cancellations and closed airports a region is willing to accept as the price of safety.
